book.title: Computer Networking: Principles, Protocols and Practice

easy.prompt: How many layers does the OSI reference model define?
easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: The OSI model has seven layers: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Three is too few — OSI splits concerns more finely than a minimal stack.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Four layers match the TCP/IP stack, not OSI.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Five layers describe the original Internet stack sketch, not the full OSI model.

easy.prompt: In the TCP/IP model, at which layer does IP operate?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Transport layer

choices.label: B
choices.body: Internet (network) layer

choices.label: C
choices.body: Application layer

choices.label: D
choices.body: Link layer

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: IP provides host-to-host datagram delivery; it sits below TCP/UDP and above link technologies.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: TCP and UDP live at transport; IP is one layer below.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Applications use TCP/UDP sockets; IP is lower in the stack.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Link layers (Ethernet, Wi-Fi) frame IP packets; IP itself is not the link layer.

easy.prompt: How many bits are in a standard IPv4 address?
easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: IPv4 addresses are 32-bit dotted-quad values, usually written as four decimal octets.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: 64 bits is common for MAC addresses, not IPv4.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: 128 bits is the size of an IPv6 address.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: 16 bits cannot uniquely identify billions of hosts on the Internet.

easy.prompt: Which transport protocol is connection-oriented and provides reliable, in-order byte delivery?

choices.label: A
choices.body: ARP

choices.label: B
choices.body: TCP

choices.label: C
choices.body: ICMP

choices.label: D
choices.body: UDP

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: TCP sets up a connection, acknowledges data, and retransmits losses; UDP is connectionless and best-effort.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: ARP resolves IP to link-layer addresses on a LAN, not end-to-end transport.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: ICMP carries control messages (e.g., ping), not application byte streams.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: UDP sends datagrams without establishing or maintaining a connection.

easy.prompt: What is the primary job of an IP router?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Terminate TLS for web clients

choices.label: B
choices.body: Assign IP addresses to hosts on a single LAN

choices.label: C
choices.body: Translate domain names to IP addresses

choices.label: D
choices.body: Forward packets between networks using routing tables

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Routers examine destination IP prefixes and choose the next hop toward the destination network.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: TLS termination is an application/proxy function, not basic IP forwarding.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That is typically DHCP on a LAN, not core routing.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: DNS resolvers perform name translation, not routers.

easy.prompt: What does the Domain Name System (DNS) primarily map?

choices.label: A
choices.body: TCP ports to process names on a host

choices.label: B
choices.body: IP addresses to MAC addresses

choices.label: C
choices.body: URLs to HTML documents

choices.label: D
choices.body: Human-readable hostnames to IP addresses

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: DNS is a distributed naming system that resolves names like www.example.com to A/AAAA records.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That is local service naming (/etc/services), not Internet DNS.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: ARP (or IPv6 ND) maps IP to link-layer addresses on a subnet.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: HTTP fetches resources; DNS only supplies name-to-address (and related) records.

easy.prompt: Which TCP port does unencrypted HTTP use by default?
easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: HTTP historically listens on port 80; HTTPS uses 443 with TLS.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Port 443 is the default for HTTPS (HTTP over TLS).
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Port 53 is reserved for DNS.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Port 22 is commonly used for SSH.

easy.prompt: Network congestion occurs when…

choices.label: A
choices.body: A host has no default gateway configured

choices.label: B
choices.body: A switch learns too many MAC addresses

choices.label: C
choices.body: Demand for bandwidth exceeds what links and buffers can carry

choices.label: D
choices.body: DNS caching expires

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Congestion is overload: queues grow, delay rises, and packets may be dropped.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Missing a gateway breaks reachability but is not congestion.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: MAC table limits affect switching, not Internet-wide bandwidth contention.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: TTL expiry causes fresh lookups, not link overload.

easy.prompt: Compared with a classic hub, an Ethernet switch…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Cannot learn MAC addresses

choices.label: B
choices.body: Operates at the network layer using IP addresses

choices.label: C
choices.body: Forwards frames only to the port leading toward the destination MAC

choices.label: D
choices.body: Broadcasts every frame to all ports always

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Switches build a MAC address table and filter traffic, reducing collisions versus a hub.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Learning source MACs per port is how switches forward efficiently.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Basic switches forward using MAC addresses at layer 2.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That describes a hub (or unknown unicast flood), not normal switched unicast.

easy.prompt: Which OSI layer is closest to where web browsers and mail clients interact with sockets?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Network

choices.label: B
choices.body: Data link

choices.label: C
choices.body: Physical

choices.label: D
choices.body: Application

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: HTTP, SMTP, and DNS are application-layer protocols accessed via transport APIs.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: IP is network layer; browsers use higher-level protocols on top of TCP.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Ethernet framing is below IP and far below HTTP.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Physical layer deals with bits on the wire, not application protocols.

easy.prompt: Which IPv4 address range is reserved for private networks (RFC 1918)?
easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: 10/8, 172.16/12, and 192.168/16 are private; they are not routed on the public Internet.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: 224/4 is multicast space, not private unicast.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: 8.8.8.x is a public anycast DNS service range, not a private block.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: 127/8 is loopback on the local host, not LAN private addressing.

easy.prompt: UDP is often chosen instead of TCP when…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Low latency matters more than guaranteed delivery (e.g., live media, DNS queries)

choices.label: B
choices.body: Every byte must arrive in order without loss

choices.label: C
choices.body: A three-way handshake is required before data

choices.label: D
choices.body: Flow control must throttle a fast sender

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: UDP exposes datagrams with no retransmission or ordering — acceptable when apps handle loss or repeat queries.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That requirement favors TCP, not UDP.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: UDP has no connection setup; TCP uses the three-way handshake.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: TCP provides window-based flow control; UDP does not.

easy.prompt: A host's default gateway is…

choices.label: A
choices.body: The DNS server that resolves all names

choices.label: B
choices.body: The router on the local subnet used to reach off-subnet destinations

choices.label: C
choices.body: The MAC address of the destination host

choices.label: D
choices.body: The longest prefix in the global BGP table

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Hosts send non-local traffic to the default gateway's IP on the LAN.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: DNS and default routing solve different problems.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Gateways are reached on-LAN; remote MACs are not known initially.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: BGP tables live in routers; hosts only need a default route.

easy.prompt: Which DNS record type maps a hostname to an IPv4 address?

choices.label: A
choices.body: A

choices.label: B
choices.body: MX

choices.label: C
choices.body: AAAA

choices.label: D
choices.body: CNAME

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: A records hold 32-bit IPv4 addresses; AAAA holds IPv6.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: MX specifies mail exchangers, not host IPv4 addresses.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: AAAA maps to IPv6, not IPv4.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: CNAME is an alias to another name, not a direct IPv4 address.

easy.prompt: An HTTP response status code of 404 means…

choices.label: A
choices.body: The client must authenticate

choices.label: B
choices.body: The server is temporarily overloaded

choices.label: C
choices.body: The request was understood and a new resource was created

choices.label: D
choices.body: The requested resource was not found on the server

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: 404 Not Found indicates the URI does not map to a resource the server can serve.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: 401/403 relate to authentication and authorization.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: 503 Service Unavailable signals overload or maintenance.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That describes 201 Created.

easy.prompt: The first packet of a TCP three-way handshake carries which flag(s)?

choices.label: A
choices.body: ACK only

choices.label: B
choices.body: RST

choices.label: C
choices.body: SYN

choices.label: D
choices.body: FIN

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: The client sends SYN; the server replies SYN-ACK; the client completes with ACK.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: ACK alone completes the handshake; it is not the opening packet.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: RST aborts a connection, it does not open one politely.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: FIN signals connection teardown, not setup.

easy.prompt: When a switch receives a frame on a port, it typically learns…

choices.label: A
choices.body: The DNS name of the host

choices.label: B
choices.body: The destination IP address of every packet

choices.label: C
choices.body: The source MAC address and associates it with that ingress port

choices.label: D
choices.body: The TCP congestion window of the sender

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Learning tables map MAC → port so future frames to that MAC can be switched unicast.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: DNS names are not present in Ethernet frame headers.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Classic switches do not parse IP for learning; they use MAC headers.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Congestion control is end-to-end transport behavior.

easy.prompt: Ethernet framing and MAC addresses belong to which OSI layer?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Physical

choices.label: B
choices.body: Network

choices.label: C
choices.body: Transport

choices.label: D
choices.body: Data link

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Layer 2 handles node-to-node delivery on a single link (e.g., Ethernet switches).

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Physical is signaling and media; framing with MACs is data link.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: IP addressing and routing are network layer.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: TCP/UDP ports are transport layer.

easy.prompt: A subnet mask in IPv4 is used to…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Resolve hostnames to IP addresses

choices.label: B
choices.body: Separate the network prefix from the host portion of an address

choices.label: C
choices.body: Encrypt packets between two hosts

choices.label: D
choices.body: Assign TCP port numbers

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Masking (or prefix length) tells hosts and routers which bits identify the subnet.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: DNS performs name resolution.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Encryption is provided by protocols like IPsec/TLS, not the mask.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Ports are transport-layer identifiers on a host.

easy.prompt: When a router's queue is full, it may…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Drop arriving packets, signaling senders to slow down

choices.label: B
choices.body: Convert TCP into UDP automatically

choices.label: C
choices.body: Disable ARP on the LAN

choices.label: D
choices.body: Increase the TCP sequence number of all flows

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Tail drops (or active queue management) cause loss that TCP interprets as congestion signals.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Routers do not change transport protocols.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: ARP is unrelated to router queue overflow.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Sequence numbers are chosen by endpoints, not routers on drop.

medium.prompt: Which pairing correctly matches a protocol to its typical TCP/IP layer?

choices.label: A
choices.body: HTTP — transport; IP — application; UDP — link

choices.label: B
choices.body: UDP — transport; IP — internet; Ethernet — link

choices.label: C
choices.body: ICMP — application; TLS — link; BGP — transport

choices.label: D
choices.body: TCP — network; DNS — physical; ARP — transport

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: End systems stack applications over TCP/UDP, then IP, then link technologies.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: HTTP is application-layer; IP is not application; UDP is not link.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: ICMP is network control; TLS sits above transport; BGP is inter-domain routing.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: TCP is transport; DNS is application; ARP is link-adjacent resolution.

medium.prompt: How many usable host addresses does a /24 IPv4 subnet have (excluding network and broadcast)?
medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: /24 leaves 8 host bits: 2^8 − 2 = 254 usable addresses on classic IPv4 subnets.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: 512 would correspond to nine host bits, not eight.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: 256 is 2^8 total addresses, but network and broadcast addresses are not assigned to hosts.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: 1022 is usable hosts in a /22, not a /24.

medium.prompt: TCP flow control primarily uses which mechanism?

choices.label: A
choices.body: TTL decrements on each hop

choices.label: B
choices.body: CNAME chains in DNS

choices.label: C
choices.body: Random early detection in routers

choices.label: D
choices.body: Receive window advertised in ACKs

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: The receiver's window tells the sender how much buffer space is available, preventing overrun.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: TTL limits packet lifetime, not sender rate to receiver buffers.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: DNS aliases do not regulate TCP sending rates.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: RED is an active queue management policy for congestion, not TCP flow control.

medium.prompt: Longest-prefix matching in a routing table means…

choices.label: A
choices.body: The first route inserted in the table wins

choices.label: B
choices.body: The route with the fewest hops always wins

choices.label: C
choices.body: Only default routes may be used

choices.label: D
choices.body: The most specific (longest) matching route wins for a destination

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: If both 10.0.0.0/8 and 10.1.0.0/16 match, the /16 route is chosen because it is longer.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Order alone does not define IP forwarding; match length does.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Hop count may matter inside a protocol, but forwarding uses prefix specificity first.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Default 0.0.0.0/0 is used only when no more-specific route matches.

medium.prompt: What is the main purpose of a DNS caching resolver?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Answer repeated queries locally using TTL-based cached records

choices.label: B
choices.body: Encrypt HTTP payloads end-to-end

choices.label: C
choices.body: Authoritatively store all Internet domain registrations

choices.label: D
choices.body: Assign MAC addresses on Wi-Fi

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Resolvers cache RRsets until TTL expires, reducing load on authoritative servers and latency.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: TLS protects HTTP; DNS may use DNSSEC but that is separate from caching.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Registrars and authoritative servers hold zone data; resolvers cache copies.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: DHCP/SLAAC and link layers handle addressing on LANs.

medium.prompt: HTTP/1.1 persistent connections allow…

choices.label: A
choices.body: UDP transport for all web pages

choices.label: B
choices.body: Automatic conversion of GET to POST

choices.label: C
choices.body: Multiple requests and responses on the same TCP connection

choices.label: D
choices.body: Only one request per TCP connection ever

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Keep-alive reuses TCP, amortizing handshake cost; pipelining/chunking evolved further in later versions.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: HTTP runs over TCP (or QUIC in HTTP/3), not classic UDP web transport.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Methods are chosen by the client; servers do not silently rewrite them.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That was common in HTTP/1.0 without Keep-Alive, not HTTP/1.1 default behavior.

medium.prompt: TCP slow start initially increases the congestion window…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Only when the receiver sends FIN

choices.label: B
choices.body: Exponentially each RTT until a threshold or loss is detected

choices.label: C
choices.body: Linearly by one MSS per RTT from the first packet

choices.label: D
choices.body: Not at all until the connection closes

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: During slow start, cwnd doubles roughly every RTT (for each ACKed segment), probing available bandwidth.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: FIN ends the connection; slow start applies at the beginning.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Linear increase is congestion avoidance after slow start or threshold.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Slow start explicitly grows the window at connection start.

medium.prompt: A broadcast domain in a switched LAN is typically…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Only hosts with public IPv4 addresses

choices.label: B
choices.body: Exactly one TCP connection

choices.label: C
choices.body: The set of ports that receive a broadcast frame (e.g., destination MAC FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF)

choices.label: D
choices.body: All routers in the global Internet

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Broadcasts flood within a VLAN/broadcast domain unless constrained by routers or L3 switches.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Private addresses still participate in LAN broadcast domains.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: TCP connections are transport-layer sessions between two endpoints.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The Internet is partitioned into many broadcast domains separated by routers.

medium.prompt: Encapsulation as data moves down the stack means…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Each layer adds its own header (and sometimes trailer) around the payload from the layer above

choices.label: B
choices.body: Only the application layer adds headers

choices.label: C
choices.body: IP addresses are replaced by MAC addresses globally

choices.label: D
choices.body: Headers are removed at every hop without change

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: A TCP segment becomes payload inside an IP datagram, which is payload inside an Ethernet frame.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Transport, network, and link layers all add headers/trailers.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: IP end-to-end identifiers remain; MACs are hop-by-hop on each link.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Headers are processed and often rewritten (e.g., TTL, MACs) per hop.

medium.prompt: Network Address Translation (NAT) on a home router allows…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Unlimited new public IPv4 addresses for every LAN host

choices.label: B
choices.body: Many private hosts to share one public IPv4 address using port translation

choices.label: C
choices.body: DNSSEC validation for all zones

choices.label: D
choices.body: IPv6-only communication without any translation

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: NAT maps (private IP, port) tuples to (public IP, port) on outbound flows and reverses inbound replies.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: NAT conserves addresses; it does not mint new public ones per host.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: DNSSEC is about DNS authenticity, not IPv4 address sharing.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: NAT64/DNS64 exist for IPv6↔IPv4, but classic NAT is an IPv4 workaround.

medium.prompt: Which field in the TCP header helps the receiver detect duplicate or out-of-order segments?

choices.label: A
choices.body: HTTP ETag

choices.label: B
choices.body: Sequence number

choices.label: C
choices.body: UDP checksum only

choices.label: D
choices.body: Ethernet type

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Sequence numbers label the byte stream so the receiver can acknowledge cumulatively and reorder.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: ETags are application-layer cache validators, not transport sequencing.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: UDP checksum covers the datagram but does not provide byte-stream ordering.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: EtherType identifies the encapsulated protocol, not TCP byte positions.

medium.prompt: Distance-vector routing protocols (e.g., RIP) advertise…

choices.label: A
choices.body: HTML cache headers

choices.label: B
choices.body: Only MAC address tables

choices.label: C
choices.body: Periodic updates of reachability metrics to neighbors

choices.label: D
choices.body: The entire link-state database to every router in the world

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Routers tell neighbors their best known distances; Bellman-Ford style computation selects paths.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Cache-Control is an HTTP concept, not a routing protocol payload.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: MAC tables are for switches on a LAN.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Link-state protocols flood topology; distance-vector shares vectors to neighbors.

medium.prompt: A DNS iterative query from a resolver to a root server typically receives…

choices.label: A
choices.body: An HTTP 301 redirect

choices.label: B
choices.body: A TCP RST

choices.label: C
choices.body: A referral to a TLD nameserver rather than the final answer

choices.label: D
choices.body: The A record for www.example.com immediately

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Iterative resolution walks the hierarchy: root → TLD → authoritative, with referrals along the way.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: HTTP redirects are unrelated to DNS iterative resolution.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: DNS runs over UDP/TCP port 53, not as arbitrary TCP resets from roots.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The root usually does not know leaf records; it delegates.

medium.prompt: An HTTP GET request is defined as…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Always carrying a JSON body that creates resources

choices.label: B
choices.body: Safe and idempotent retrieval of a representation (should not change server state by convention)

choices.label: C
choices.body: A replacement for DNS A queries

choices.label: D
choices.body: Encrypted by TLS inside the TCP header

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: GET fetches resources; side effects belong in POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE per method semantics.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Bodies on GET are discouraged; creation uses POST/PUT.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: DNS resolves names; HTTP requests resources from servers.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: TLS encrypts the connection above TCP; it is not inside the TCP header.

medium.prompt: Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) allows routers to…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Mark IP packets instead of dropping them, signaling congestion to TCP endpoints

choices.label: B
choices.body: Disable TCP acknowledgments

choices.label: C
choices.body: Bypass DNS entirely

choices.label: D
choices.body: Increase link speed automatically

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: ECN-capable routers set CE bits; TCP reacts similarly to loss without always discarding packets.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: TCP still ACKs; ECN modifies how congestion is signaled.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: ECN is an IP/TCP feature unrelated to name resolution.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: ECN does not change physical link rates.

medium.prompt: Spanning Tree Protocol (STP) on switches prevents…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Bridging loops that would cause broadcast storms

choices.label: B
choices.body: HTTPS certificate expiration

choices.label: C
choices.body: IP address exhaustion on the Internet

choices.label: D
choices.body: TCP three-way handshakes from completing

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: STP blocks redundant paths logically so only one active tree forwards frames between segments.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Certificates are application/TLS concerns.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That is an addressing/policy issue, not a layer-2 loop issue.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: STP affects Ethernet topology, not TCP state machines directly.

medium.prompt: The TCP checksum covers which parts (conceptually)?

choices.label: A
choices.body: TCP header, payload, and a pseudo-header with IP addresses and protocol

choices.label: B
choices.body: Only the Ethernet FCS

choices.label: C
choices.body: Only the HTTP response body

choices.label: D
choices.body: Only the DNS query name

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: The pseudo-header ties the segment to the IP endpoints so misdelivery corrupts the checksum.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: FCS protects the frame on the wire; TCP has its own end-to-end checksum.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: HTTP is payload inside TCP; TCP checksum covers more than application data alone.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: DNS over UDP/TCP has its own checks; TCP checksum is transport-wide.

medium.prompt: Link-state routing (e.g., OSPF) requires each router to…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Flood reliable link-state advertisements and run Dijkstra locally

choices.label: B
choices.body: Learn routes exclusively from DHCP

choices.label: C
choices.body: Exchange only hop counts with no topology map

choices.label: D
choices.body: Use HTTP caching headers to pick paths

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: With a consistent LSDB, each router computes shortest paths independently using link weights.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: DHCP may give hosts a default route, not intra-domain OSPF topology.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That describes distance-vector style updates, not full link-state flooding.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Routing protocols do not use HTTP cache directives.

medium.prompt: DNS over UDP typically uses truncation (TC bit) when…

choices.label: A
choices.body: A switch MAC table overflows

choices.label: B
choices.body: The response is too large for UDP, prompting retry over TCP

choices.label: C
choices.body: HTTP returns status 500

choices.label: D
choices.body: The client sends a SYN packet

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Large responses (many records) exceed UDP payload limits; TCP DNS carries the full message.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Switch scaling issues do not set the DNS TC bit.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: HTTP errors are unrelated to DNS TC.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: SYN is TCP connection setup, not a DNS UDP field.

medium.prompt: The Host header in HTTP/1.1 is important because…

choices.label: A
choices.body: It encrypts the request body

choices.label: B
choices.body: It specifies the authority (hostname) for virtual hosting on a shared IP

choices.label: C
choices.body: It stores the client's MAC address

choices.label: D

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Multiple sites can share one IP; Host tells the server which name the client intended.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: TLS encrypts; Host is cleartext metadata in HTTP/1.1.

hard.prompt: Why is strict OSI layering often blurred in real implementations (e.g., TCP checksum pseudo-header)?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Because Ethernet switches must parse HTTP headers

choices.label: B
choices.body: Because DNS runs below the physical layer

choices.label: C
choices.body: Practical stacks violate pure layering for performance and end-to-end integrity

choices.label: D
choices.body: Because IP is actually an application protocol

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Cross-layer information (pseudo-header, offload, QUIC in user space) trades purity for speed and correctness.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Switches need not parse HTTP for basic forwarding.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: DNS is application-layer naming, above transport.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: IP remains network-layer datagram delivery.

hard.prompt: IPv6 Stateless Address Autoconfiguration (SLAAC) combines…

choices.label: A

choices.label: B
choices.body: Router Advertisements (prefix) with interface identifiers (often EUI-64 or privacy extensions)

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

hard.explanation: Hosts learn prefixes from RA messages and form addresses without a DHCP server for basic connectivity.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Those are IPv4/Ethernet mechanisms, not IPv6 SLAAC.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Web protocols do not configure IPv6 addressing.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: BGP is inter-domain routing between routers, not host autoconfig.

hard.prompt: TCP Reno reacts to a timeout (RTO) primarily by…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Immediately closing the connection with FIN

choices.label: B
choices.body: Setting ssthresh to cwnd/2, resetting cwnd to 1 MSS, and retransmitting the earliest unACKed segment

choices.label: C
choices.body: Ignoring loss because cumulative ACKs always recover

choices.label: D
choices.body: Switching to UDP for the rest of the flow

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Timeout implies severe congestion; Reno collapses the window and begins slow start again.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Timeouts trigger retransmit and window collapse, not mandatory FIN.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Timeouts exist precisely when ACK-based recovery is insufficient.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Transport protocol does not change mid-connection.

hard.prompt: BGP path selection between two valid routes to the same prefix typically considers (among other knobs)…

choices.label: A

choices.label: B
choices.body: Local policy attributes (LOCAL_PREF, AS_PATH length, MED) before installing a route

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: BGP is policy-driven inter-domain routing; attribute comparison implements operator preferences.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: DNS TTL does not influence BGP best-path selection.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: BGP runs between routers, not from browser headers.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Physical appearance is irrelevant to BGP decision processes.

hard.prompt: DNSSEC primarily provides…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Authentication and integrity of DNS data via chained signatures, not confidentiality

choices.label: B
choices.body: Automatic NAT traversal for TCP

choices.label: C
choices.body: Encryption of all DNS queries so ISPs cannot see QNAMEs

choices.label: D
choices.body: Replacement of TCP congestion control

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: DNSSEC signs RRsets; resolvers validate from trust anchors. QNAMEs may still leak without DNS-over-TLS/HTTPS.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: NAT traversal uses other mechanisms (STUN/ICE), not DNSSEC.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Privacy needs DoT/DoH; DNSSEC does not encrypt queries by default.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: DNSSEC is unrelated to transport congestion algorithms.

hard.prompt: HTTP/2 multiplexing improves on HTTP/1.1 chiefly by…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Sending all resources over UDP port 53

choices.label: B
choices.body: Eliminating TLS entirely

choices.label: C
choices.body: Opening a new TCP connection per image unconditionally

choices.label: D
choices.body: Interleaving many streams over one TCP connection with binary framing and stream IDs

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: HTTP/2 avoids head-of-line blocking at the HTTP layer (though TCP HOL remains until HTTP/3/QUIC).

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: HTTP/2 still runs over TCP/TLS in common deployments, not DNS UDP.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: HTTPS still uses TLS; HTTP/2 is often negotiated inside TLS ALPN.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That was an HTTP/1.1 workaround; HTTP/2 reduces parallel connections.

hard.prompt: TCP Cubic (common on Linux) models its window growth with a cubic function primarily to…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Guarantee zero packet loss on the Internet

choices.label: B
choices.body: Replace IP routing tables on every ACK

choices.label: C
choices.body: Disable slow start permanently

choices.label: D
choices.body: Scale aggressively on high-bandwidth-delay-product paths while probing fairly after loss

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Cubic targets W_max-dependent growth for high BDP links, improving throughput versus linear Reno on fat pipes.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Loss still occurs; Cubic adapts rates, it cannot eliminate congestion.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Routing is separate; Cubic only adjusts sender congestion window.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Connections still begin with slow start; Cubic governs congestion avoidance growth.

hard.prompt: VLANs (802.1Q) allow a single physical switch fabric to…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Assign TCP port 443 to every host

choices.label: B
choices.body: Route IP packets between continents without routers

choices.label: C
choices.body: Encrypt TCP payloads at layer 2 by default

choices.label: D

hard.explanation: 802.1Q tags carry VLAN IDs so ports can participate in multiple logical LANs securely segmented.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Port numbers are transport endpoints on hosts, not VLAN tags.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Inter-VLAN routing still needs a router or L3 switch.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: VLANs segment traffic; encryption is not their primary function.

hard.prompt: The primary reason QUIC (HTTP/3) moves reliability into user space over UDP is to…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Make DNS iterative queries obsolete

choices.label: B
choices.body: Eliminate the need for IP addresses

choices.label: C
choices.body: Avoid using any encryption on the web

choices.label: D
choices.body: Reduce transport-layer head-of-line blocking and enable faster connection establishment with integrated TLS

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: QUIC multiplexes streams with independent loss recovery and combines crypto with setup, unlike single-byte-stream TCP.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: HTTP still relies on DNS (or alternatives like DoH) for naming.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: QUIC still runs over IP (v4 or v6).
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: QUIC mandates TLS 1.3 integration for security.

hard.prompt: CIDR aggregation in the global routing table helps providers…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Advertise a shorter prefix covering many customer subnets, shrinking table size

choices.label: B
choices.body: Remove the need for default routes on hosts

choices.label: C
choices.body: Store MAC addresses inside DNS A records

choices.label: D
choices.body: Assign duplicate public IPv4 addresses to different continents safely

hard.explanation: Summarization (e.g., aggregating /24s into a /16 announcement) reduces BGP churn and memory.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Hosts still need defaults to reach non-local prefixes.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: A records hold IP addresses, not Ethernet MACs.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Public addresses must remain globally unique.

hard.prompt: Selective Acknowledgments (SACK) in TCP allow the sender to…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Run without any receiver window

choices.label: B
choices.body: Retransmit only missing segments when multiple disjoint ranges are outstanding

choices.label: C
choices.body: Send data without ever numbering bytes

choices.label: D
choices.body: Ignore all losses after the first duplicate ACK

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: SACK blocks in options describe non-contiguous received data, improving recovery on multiple losses.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Flow control still uses the receive window alongside SACK.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Sequence numbers are still fundamental to TCP.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Duplicate ACKs trigger fast retransmit; SACK refines which segments to resend.

hard.prompt: Equal-cost multi-path (ECMP) forwarding sends flows along different next hops by often hashing…

choices.label: A

choices.label: B
choices.body: The DNS TTL value alone

choices.label: C
choices.body: Only the HTTP Server header

choices.label: D
choices.body: Five-tuple (src/dst IP, protocol, ports) so packets of a flow stay on one path

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Per-flow hashing preserves ordering within a TCP connection while utilizing parallel links.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: WAN routing uses IP forwarding; MACs change per hop on L2 segments.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: TTL in DNS records is unrelated to router ECMP hash keys.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Routers forward on IP headers before HTTP is visible (if at all).

hard.prompt: A DNS negative cache entry (NXDOMAIN) prevents…

choices.label: A

choices.label: B

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

hard.explanation: Resolvers cache failures as well as successes, reducing load during typos or attacks.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Negative DNS caching does not alter TCP congestion algorithms.

wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Certificates are validated in TLS, not by DNS negative caching.

hard.prompt: HTTP conditional GET with If-None-Match: <etag> can yield status 304 when…

choices.label: A

hard.prompt: Bufferbloat is problematic because large router queues…

choices.label: D

wrongAnswerExplanations.d: MAC learning is independent of WAN queue sizing.

hard.prompt: Cut-through switching differs from store-and-forward because it…

hard.prompt: SYN cookies mitigate SYN flood attacks by…
